parent_passage.text:
I. Radiography chest
Although chest radiography is not sensitive or specific for detecting suspected DLD, it is often used
as an initial test to detect alternative diagnoses, such as infection or cardiogenic edema (see the
ACR Appropriateness Criteria® topics on “Acute Respiratory Illness in Immunocompetent
Patients” [4], “Acute Respiratory Illness in Immunocompromised Patients” [5] , “Chronic Dyspnea-
Noncardiovascular Origin” [7], and “Rib Fractures” [30] for further guidance). Obtaining a baseline
chest radiograph at time of initial diagnosis of DLD may assist with diagnosis of these other
conditions via radiography on follow-up [31]. A normal chest radiograph in the setting of
suspected DLD does not exclude the possibility of clinically important DLD [32]. Multiple studies
demonstrate the increased sensitivity and specificity of CT over radiographs for evaluation of DLD

observations.value: Confluent opacities are present in both mid and lower lung zones bilaterally on the PA view (Figure 1a), with relative sparing of the upper lobes.
The density and extent of consolidation appear relatively symmetric between left and right lungs on the PA view; no clear unilateral predominance is visible.
The lateral view (Figure 1b) and its crop show dense, confluent opacities in the posterior basal regions, consistent with bilateral posterior-basal predominant consolidation.
Upper lung zones appear relatively spared; no significant consolidation is evident in the apical or upper zones on either PA or lateral views.
